304.history: An ancient ford in the north-west near a quarry of green stone, whose polished axes were carried all over the island in the three thousand four hundred and ninety-sixth year, too fine for work, laid unused in graves and under house floors. Ìomhar Dearg asked the cutters for one to carry and use and was told no green axe was ever cut to be swung, only shown; he had a common grey axe made instead and used it forty years. The few households who worked the quarry traded in nothing else, and the chips about it lay knee-deep. The seam ran thin under every cut, and in the three thousand five hundred and forty-seventh year the last cutter who held the old skill died with no apprentice; the quarry was forsaken, and the axes ceased.

371.history: A settlement on the lower Abhainn ìseal by the skerries off the river mouth, where the households took seals by agreement, one household to a rock in its own turn, kept on notched sticks. A rock taken out of turn was the commonest quarrel of that coast, settled always by counting the tally aloud rather than by raised voices.

20.history: A settlement on the bank of the Abhainn ìseal a short walk from the old standing stone. The generation that settled it in the three thousand nine hundred and eighth year set its houses, by no law anyone could name, so that no door faced the stone, and every household built after kept the same pattern unquestioned.

395.history: A field country near Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh in the east, where in the four thousand and eighth year a household cleared and banked the widest single field the eastern country had yet cut from the rough, the largest of the age. It laid its bank on the stones of an older wall whose builders none could name, and grew in a good year wheat enough for three households where before there had been land for none.
395.known_for: the widest field of the age

145.history: A settlement in the north beside a spring held sacred, whose settlers led the water round in channels of their own digging and fenced the spring before a single wall was raised, so that a stranger coming on the place might take the water, and not the people, for what had been settled there. They watered their fields from the channels and would not build over the spring.
145.known_for: the spring fenced before any house

443.history: A settlement on the rough strait of the north-east coast, taken up in the four thousand one hundred and twenty-eighth year by households who fished the strait in skin boats. They laid paddles beside their dead, and their boats were heavier in the beam than any on that coast, for the strait's sake. Its fishers named their boats for the winds as the north coast did, and gave no drowned boat's name again. In the lean years they brought dried fish inland to the sharing, and a household that kept its catch back found no boat willing to put out beside it the next season.
443.known_for: the paddles laid beside the dead

333.history: A settlement that grew up under the dark oaks in the north in the four thousand one hundred and eighty-third year. Its people penned pigs in the wood and drove them out to the acorns at the fall of the year, and felled no oak they could spare. The households of the dark oaks kept the full hand at their hearths like every settlement of the hills, and sent their measure to be tried against a copy of the stone cup when the lot for the slab came to be drawn from every part of the hills. Their pigs went to the ford in the autumns, driven the whole way on foot.

197.history: An old river port on the narrows of the Abhainn ìseal east of the vein. In the four thousand and fifty-eighth year two households quarrelling over a stretch of the landing sat out a night together and gave the ground to the landing itself, for whoever had a boat drawn up there; within two generations they were thoroughly mixed by marriage. By the four thousand two hundred and twenty-eighth year it was the river landing of the hill households of the east, where salt, fish and seal-skins came up from the coast; a cloth-trader passing through told the child Ailis of the young-faced man at the gate of Dùn ìseal, and she married a net-mender of the landing.
197.known_for: the landing given to no one
